tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

Done. Here’s what I’ve set up and verified:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
    - containerPort: 80 (matches stable)
  - Pod spec securityContext: {} (matches stable)

Traffic routing change
- Updated Service recommendation-engine selector from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods.
- Service port config preserved: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged).

Verification
- Pods (2 stable + 2 canary) are Running:
  - engine-v2-0-... (v2.0) x2
  - engine-v2-1-... (v2.1) x2
- Endpoints for recommendation-engine now include 4 addresses (2 from each deployment), so traffic will be approximately 50/50 across stable and canary.

Notes and quick rollback options
- To revert to 0% canary: either
  - Change Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or
  - Scale engine-v2-1 replicas to 0, or
  - Delete the engine-v2-1 deployment.
- To adjust the canary percentage without changing the Service, modify replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ~25% canary). For precise weighting, consider an ingress/gateway or service mesh.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I’ve set up and verified:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
    - containerPort: 80 (matches stable)
  - Pod spec securityContext: {} (matches stable)

Traffic routing change
- Updated Service recommendation-engine selector from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods.
- Service port config preserved: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged).

Verification
- Pods (2 stable + 2 canary) are Running:
  - engine-v2-0-... (v2.0) x2
  - engine-v2-1-... (v2.1) x2
- Endpoints for recommendation-engine now include 4 addresses (2 from each deployment), so traffic will be approximately 50/50 across stable and canary.

Notes and quick rollback options
- To revert to 0% canary: either
  - Change Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or
  - Scale engine-v2-1 replicas to 0, or
  - Delete the engine-v2-1 deployment.
- To adjust the canary percentage without changing the Service, modify replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ~25% canary). For precise weighting, consider an ingress/gateway or service mesh.

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which doesn’t exist. The PVC was stuck in Pending, so the pod couldn’t be scheduled.
- What I changed: Deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it using the existing default StorageClass "standard".
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi, RWO).
  - Pod homepage-pod in namespace homepage-ns is Running and Ready.
  - Pod details: container nginx started and is ready; phase: Running; IP: 10.244.0.23.

Notes:
- Deleting the PVC was safe here because it was never bound (no data to lose).
- If you intended to use a different StorageClass, let me know the correct name and I can switch the PVC accordingly.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

Fixed.

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which doesn’t exist. The PVC was stuck in Pending, so the pod couldn’t be scheduled.
- What I changed: Deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it using the existing default StorageClass "standard".
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi, RWO).
  - Pod homepage-pod in namespace homepage-ns is Running and Ready.
  - Pod details: container nginx started and is ready; phase: Running; IP: 10.244.0.23.

Notes:
- Deleting the PVC was safe here because it was never bound (no data to lose).
- If you intended to use a different StorageClass, let me know the correct name and I can switch the PVC accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which doesn’t exist. The PVC was stuck in Pending, so the pod couldn’t be scheduled.
- What I changed: Deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it using the existing default StorageClass "standard".
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi, RWO).
  - Pod homepage-pod in namespace homepage-ns is Running and Ready.
  - Pod details: container nginx started and is ready; phase: Running; IP: 10.244.0.23.

Notes:
- Deleting the PVC was safe here because it was never bound (no data to lose).
- If you intended to use a different StorageClass, let me know the correct name and I can switch the PVC accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but:
  - The liveness/readiness probes were checking HTTP on port 80 (and custom paths /get_status and /is_ready), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now check GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - Port 80 now targets containerPort 8080.

Current status
- Deployment orders/webapp: Available 1/1.
- Pod orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-5v9wz: Ready 1/1.
- Service orders/webapp: ClusterIP 10.102.247.4, port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints show the pod registered and ready on 8080.
- Health probes are returning 200.

How to access
- Inside the cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (or use the Service name webapp in the orders namespace).
- There’s no Ingress configured. If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service—just say which you prefer.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but:
  - The liveness/readiness probes were checking HTTP on port 80 (and custom paths /get_status and /is_ready), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now check GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - Port 80 now targets containerPort 8080.

Current status
- Deployment orders/webapp: Available 1/1.
- Pod orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-5v9wz: Ready 1/1.
- Service orders/webapp: ClusterIP 10.102.247.4, port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints show the pod registered and ready on 8080.
- Health probes are returning 200.

How to access
- Inside the cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (or use the Service name webapp in the orders namespace).
- There’s no Ingress configured. If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service—just say which you prefer.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but:
  - The liveness/readiness probes were checking HTTP on port 80 (and custom paths /get_status and /is_ready), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now check GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - Port 80 now targets containerPort 8080.

Current status
- Deployment orders/webapp: Available 1/1.
- Pod orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-5v9wz: Ready 1/1.
- Service orders/webapp: ClusterIP 10.102.247.4, port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints show the pod registered and ready on 8080.
- Health probes are returning 200.

How to access
- Inside the cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (or use the Service name webapp in the orders namespace).
- There’s no Ingress configured. If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service—just say which you prefer.

Success: Pod is now Ready

Success: Pod is stable with acceptable number of restarts

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/v1 Deployments, not core/v1 Pods. So the pod-reader SA had no permission to list Pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 Pods.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
  - Kept the existing apps/v1 Deployments list rule.

Current state
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader
- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role now grants get/list/watch on Pods
- RoleBinding: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding correctly binds the SA to the Role

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  - Expected: yes
- kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Notes
- This permission applies only within the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list Pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding instead.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty (no backing Pods), so the Service had nothing to route to.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80:
  - nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 (confirmed inside the Pod).
  - Result: Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - Selector set to app=nginx (to match the Deployment)
  - targetPort set to 8080 (to match the container)
- Result now:
  - Endpoints for Service nginx show the Pod IP and port 8080
  - In-Pod test returns HTTP 200 when calling http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

Verification evidence
- Before: Endpoints were empty for Service nginx.
- After:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.27:8080
  - From the nginx Pod: curl to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned 200.

Notes and next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible inside the cluster. If you tried from outside, it will not work by design. To expose externally, choose one:
  - Port-forward: kubectl -n web port-forward deploy/nginx 8080:8080 and browse http://localhost:8080
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web expose deploy nginx --type=NodePort --name=nginx-nodeport --port=80 --target-port=8080
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it): change Service type to LoadBalancer
  - Ingress: create an Ingress pointing to Service nginx port 80

Optional cleanups (not required, but recommended)
- Add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment spec for clarity.
- Add readiness/liveness probes on port 8080.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty (no backing Pods), so the Service had nothing to route to.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80:
  - nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 (confirmed inside the Pod).
  - Result: Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - Selector set to app=nginx (to match the Deployment)
  - targetPort set to 8080 (to match the container)
- Result now:
  - Endpoints for Service nginx show the Pod IP and port 8080
  - In-Pod test returns HTTP 200 when calling http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

Verification evidence
- Before: Endpoints were empty for Service nginx.
- After:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.27:8080
  - From the nginx Pod: curl to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned 200.

Notes and next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible inside the cluster. If you tried from outside, it will not work by design. To expose externally, choose one:
  - Port-forward: kubectl -n web port-forward deploy/nginx 8080:8080 and browse http://localhost:8080
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web expose deploy nginx --type=NodePort --name=nginx-nodeport --port=80 --target-port=8080
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it): change Service type to LoadBalancer
  - Ingress: create an Ingress pointing to Service nginx port 80

Optional cleanups (not required, but recommended)
- Add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment spec for clarity.
- Add readiness/liveness probes on port 8080.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty (no backing Pods), so the Service had nothing to route to.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80:
  - nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 (confirmed inside the Pod).
  - Result: Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - Selector set to app=nginx (to match the Deployment)
  - targetPort set to 8080 (to match the container)
- Result now:
  - Endpoints for Service nginx show the Pod IP and port 8080
  - In-Pod test returns HTTP 200 when calling http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

Verification evidence
- Before: Endpoints were empty for Service nginx.
- After:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.27:8080
  - From the nginx Pod: curl to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned 200.

Notes and next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible inside the cluster. If you tried from outside, it will not work by design. To expose externally, choose one:
  - Port-forward: kubectl -n web port-forward deploy/nginx 8080:8080 and browse http://localhost:8080
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web expose deploy nginx --type=NodePort --name=nginx-nodeport --port=80 --target-port=8080
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it): change Service type to LoadBalancer
  - Ingress: create an Ingress pointing to Service nginx port 80

Optional cleanups (not required, but recommended)
- Add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment spec for clarity.
- Add readiness/liveness probes on port 8080.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Pods not running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Connection refused: The nginx container is listening on port 8080 (per /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf: listen 8080;), while the Service was targeting port 80. That made the Service forward to a closed port, causing connection refused.

What I changed to fix it
1) Scheduling fix
- Removed the restrictive nodeSelector from the Deployment. The previous server-side apply retained it, so I deleted and recreated the Deployment without nodeSelector.
- Result: 2 pods are now Running on the node.
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-qp5mp (Running, IP 10.244.0.33)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-mvjrt (Running, IP 10.244.0.34)

2) Service port fix
- Updated Service web-app-service to map port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Result: Endpoints now point to the pods on port 8080:
  - 10.244.0.33:8080
  - 10.244.0.34:8080

Current status (webshop-frontend)
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2 replicas running.
- Service web-app-service: ClusterIP, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, endpoints healthy.

Impact
- There was a brief restart while replacing the Deployment to remove the nodeSelector.
- Traffic via http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should now succeed.

Recommendations
- If you intended to pin these pods to special nodes, either:
  - Label the target node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Or use nodeAffinity with clear fallbacks.
- Align metadata for clarity:
  - Update containerPort in the Deployment to 8080 (optional; current setup works since Service targets 8080).
- Add health probes to improve rollout safety:
  - readinessProbe: TCP or HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - livenessProbe: TCP or HTTP GET / on port 8080

Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Pods not running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Connection refused: The nginx container is listening on port 8080 (per /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf: listen 8080;), while the Service was targeting port 80. That made the Service forward to a closed port, causing connection refused.

What I changed to fix it
1) Scheduling fix
- Removed the restrictive nodeSelector from the Deployment. The previous server-side apply retained it, so I deleted and recreated the Deployment without nodeSelector.
- Result: 2 pods are now Running on the node.
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-qp5mp (Running, IP 10.244.0.33)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-mvjrt (Running, IP 10.244.0.34)

2) Service port fix
- Updated Service web-app-service to map port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Result: Endpoints now point to the pods on port 8080:
  - 10.244.0.33:8080
  - 10.244.0.34:8080

Current status (webshop-frontend)
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2 replicas running.
- Service web-app-service: ClusterIP, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, endpoints healthy.

Impact
- There was a brief restart while replacing the Deployment to remove the nodeSelector.
- Traffic via http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should now succeed.

Recommendations
- If you intended to pin these pods to special nodes, either:
  - Label the target node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Or use nodeAffinity with clear fallbacks.
- Align metadata for clarity:
  - Update containerPort in the Deployment to 8080 (optional; current setup works since Service targets 8080).
- Add health probes to improve rollout safety:
  - readinessProbe: TCP or HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - livenessProbe: TCP or HTTP GET / on port 8080

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Pods not running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Connection refused: The nginx container is listening on port 8080 (per /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf: listen 8080;), while the Service was targeting port 80. That made the Service forward to a closed port, causing connection refused.

What I changed to fix it
1) Scheduling fix
- Removed the restrictive nodeSelector from the Deployment. The previous server-side apply retained it, so I deleted and recreated the Deployment without nodeSelector.
- Result: 2 pods are now Running on the node.
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-qp5mp (Running, IP 10.244.0.33)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-mvjrt (Running, IP 10.244.0.34)

2) Service port fix
- Updated Service web-app-service to map port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Result: Endpoints now point to the pods on port 8080:
  - 10.244.0.33:8080
  - 10.244.0.34:8080

Current status (webshop-frontend)
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2 replicas running.
- Service web-app-service: ClusterIP, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, endpoints healthy.

Impact
- There was a brief restart while replacing the Deployment to remove the nodeSelector.
- Traffic via http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should now succeed.

Recommendations
- If you intended to pin these pods to special nodes, either:
  - Label the target node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Or use nodeAffinity with clear fallbacks.
- Align metadata for clarity:
  - Update containerPort in the Deployment to 8080 (optional; current setup works since Service targets 8080).
- Add health probes to improve rollout safety:
  - readinessProbe: TCP or HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - livenessProbe: TCP or HTTP GET / on port 8080

Want me to align containerPort to 8080 and add basic liveness/readiness probes?

Done. I created the Pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace.

What I set up:
- Two containers in spec.containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, exposes port 8080, mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox, runs: sh -c "touch /var/log/nginx/access.log && tail -n+1 -f /var/log/nginx/access.log", mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Readiness: Pod is considered ready when the web server serves traffic via an HTTP readinessProbe on / at port 8080

Current state:
- Pod phase: Running
- Both containers Ready

How to verify:
- kubectl get pod -n multi-container-logging communication-pod
- kubectl logs -n multi-container-logging pod/communication-pod -c logger --tail=50
- Optional traffic test:
  - kubectl -n multi-container-logging port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080
  - curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/

outputSteps.content:
Done. I created the Pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace.

What I set up:
- Two containers in spec.containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, exposes port 8080, mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox, runs: sh -c "touch /var/log/nginx/access.log && tail -n+1 -f /var/log/nginx/access.log", mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Readiness: Pod is considered ready when the web server serves traffic via an HTTP readinessProbe on / at port 8080

Current state:
- Pod phase: Running
- Both containers Ready

How to verify:
- kubectl get pod -n multi-container-logging communication-pod
- kubectl logs -n multi-container-logging pod/communication-pod -c logger --tail=50
- Optional traffic test:
  - kubectl -n multi-container-logging port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080
  - curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/

- kubectl exec -n resize-pv storage-pod -- sh -lc 'df -h /usr/share/nginx/html'

Steps.message:
namespace/resize-pv created
persistentvolumeclaim/storage-pvc created
pod/storage-pod created

Done. The volume used by storage-pod (PVC storage-pvc) in namespace resize-pv has been resized to 3Gi and the pod was restarted to complete the filesystem resize.

What I did:
- Confirmed the StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc allows expansion.
- Updated the PVC storage request from 1Gi to 3Gi.
- Observed FileSystemResizePending on the PVC, so I recreated storage-pod to trigger node-level filesystem resize.
- Verified PVC status capacity is now 3Gi and the pod is Running.

If you want to double-check from inside the container, you can run:
- kubectl exec -n resize-pv storage-pod -- sh -lc 'df -h /usr/share/nginx/html'

results.taskOutput:
The multi-tenant development environment has been created and configured according to your requirements. Below is what was provisioned and how it maps to each requirement, plus quick verification steps and notes.

What I created

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=alice)
- dev-bob (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=bob)
- dev-charlie (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=charlie)
- dev-shared (labels: env=dev, role=shared, access=dev-shared)
- staging (labels: env=staging, tenant=ops)
- prod (labels: env=prod, tenant=ops)

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa

- Full access (own namespace) for each developer and their SA:
  - Role namespace-owner created in each dev namespace granting full verbs on namespaced resources.
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace bind namespace-owner to:
    - the corresponding user (alice, bob, charlie)
    - the corresponding SA (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)

- Read-only access to dev-shared for developers and their SAs:
  - Role readonly created in dev-shared with get/list/watch on all resources.
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly-users in dev-shared binds Role readonly to users alice, bob, charlie.
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly-sas in dev-shared binds Role readonly to ServiceAccounts:
    - dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie/charlie-sa

- Access to staging and prod:
  - No RoleBindings were created for developers in staging or prod. Only cluster-admins (or any pre-existing admin bindings you have) can access those namespaces.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
  - requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
  - requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi
  - requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation + allowed paths)
Default deny + explicit allows were created in all six namespaces.

- Dev namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-same-ns-and-shared:
    - Ingress: only from same namespace and from dev-shared
    - Egress: only to same namespace and to dev-shared
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system (CoreDNS)
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (ClusterIP 10.96.0.1)

- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-dev-tenants-and-same-ns:
    - Ingress: from namespaces labeled tenant=dev and from dev-shared itself
    - Egress: to namespaces labeled tenant=dev and to dev-shared itself
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (10.96.0.1)

- staging and prod:
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-same-namespace only (no access to or from dev namespaces)
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (10.96.0.1)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented default-deny for all non-system namespaces created above.
- No policies were added to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system).

How this meets your requirements

- Namespaces: all six created as requested.
- RBAC:
  - Each developer and their SA have full access to only their own namespace.
  - Developers and their SAs have read-only access to dev-shared.
  - No developer access granted to staging/prod; only cluster admins retain access.
- Resource quotas: enforced exactly per your limits for each namespace category.
- Network policies:
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked by default-deny and only-allow rules.
  - Dev namespaces can communicate with dev-shared, but not with each other.
  - All namespaces can resolve DNS (egress to kube-system:53) and reach the API server.
  - staging/prod are isolated from dev by only allowing same-namespace traffic.
- Default deny: applied across all non-system namespaces for least privilege.

Verification commands

- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- ServiceAccounts:
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-charlie
- RBAC:
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-charlie
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-shared
- Resource quotas:
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-shared -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n staging -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n prod -o yaml
- Network policies:
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-charlie
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-shared
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n staging
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n prod

Notes and recommendations

- NetworkPolicy support: Ensure your CNI plugin enforces NetworkPolicies (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Weave Net). If you use a CNI without NetworkPolicy support, these isolation rules won’t take effect.
- Developer identities: This setup assumes your cluster authentication maps users alice, bob, and charlie to those Kubernetes User identities (e.g., via OIDC or certificates). If you use groups, we can swap user subjects for group subjects.
- Image pulls: Default-deny policies do not affect image pulls (done by the kubelet), so they will continue to work.
- Optional hardening:
  - Add LimitRanges in each namespace to enforce default resource requests/limits and max per-container.
  - Consider PodSecurity admission or PSA labels to restrict pod security levels in dev vs staging/prod.
  - If developers need specific egress (e.g., to external services), we can add targeted Egress rules per namespace.

If you’d like, I can export all applied manifests into a single bundle for version control, or tailor the RBAC to use groups (e.g., devs) instead of individual users.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

The multi-tenant development environment has been created and configured according to your requirements. Below is what was provisioned and how it maps to each requirement, plus quick verification steps and notes.

What I created

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=alice)
- dev-bob (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=bob)
- dev-charlie (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=charlie)
- dev-shared (labels: env=dev, role=shared, access=dev-shared)
- staging (labels: env=staging, tenant=ops)
- prod (labels: env=prod, tenant=ops)

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa

- Full access (own namespace) for each developer and their SA:
  - Role namespace-owner created in each dev namespace granting full verbs on namespaced resources.
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace bind namespace-owner to:
    - the corresponding user (alice, bob, charlie)
    - the corresponding SA (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)

- Read-only access to dev-shared for developers and their SAs:
  - Role readonly created in dev-shared with get/list/watch on all resources.
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly-users in dev-shared binds Role readonly to users alice, bob, charlie.
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly-sas in dev-shared binds Role readonly to ServiceAccounts:
    - dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie/charlie-sa

- Access to staging and prod:
  - No RoleBindings were created for developers in staging or prod. Only cluster-admins (or any pre-existing admin bindings you have) can access those namespaces.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
  - requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
  - requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi
  - requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation + allowed paths)
Default deny + explicit allows were created in all six namespaces.

- Dev namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-same-ns-and-shared:
    - Ingress: only from same namespace and from dev-shared
    - Egress: only to same namespace and to dev-shared
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system (CoreDNS)
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (ClusterIP 10.96.0.1)

- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-dev-tenants-and-same-ns:
    - Ingress: from namespaces labeled tenant=dev and from dev-shared itself
    - Egress: to namespaces labeled tenant=dev and to dev-shared itself
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (10.96.0.1)

- staging and prod:
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-same-namespace only (no access to or from dev namespaces)
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (10.96.0.1)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented default-deny for all non-system namespaces created above.
- No policies were added to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system).

How this meets your requirements

- Namespaces: all six created as requested.
- RBAC:
  - Each developer and their SA have full access to only their own namespace.
  - Developers and their SAs have read-only access to dev-shared.
  - No developer access granted to staging/prod; only cluster admins retain access.
- Resource quotas: enforced exactly per your limits for each namespace category.
- Network policies:
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked by default-deny and only-allow rules.
  - Dev namespaces can communicate with dev-shared, but not with each other.
  - All namespaces can resolve DNS (egress to kube-system:53) and reach the API server.
  - staging/prod are isolated from dev by only allowing same-namespace traffic.
- Default deny: applied across all non-system namespaces for least privilege.

Verification commands

- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- ServiceAccounts:
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-charlie
- RBAC:
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-charlie
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-shared
- Resource quotas:
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-shared -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n staging -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n prod -o yaml
- Network policies:
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-charlie
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-shared
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n staging
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n prod

Notes and recommendations

- NetworkPolicy support: Ensure your CNI plugin enforces NetworkPolicies (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Weave Net). If you use a CNI without NetworkPolicy support, these isolation rules won’t take effect.
- Developer identities: This setup assumes your cluster authentication maps users alice, bob, and charlie to those Kubernetes User identities (e.g., via OIDC or certificates). If you use groups, we can swap user subjects for group subjects.
- Image pulls: Default-deny policies do not affect image pulls (done by the kubelet), so they will continue to work.
- Optional hardening:
  - Add LimitRanges in each namespace to enforce default resource requests/limits and max per-container.
  - Consider PodSecurity admission or PSA labels to restrict pod security levels in dev vs staging/prod.
  - If developers need specific egress (e.g., to external services), we can add targeted Egress rules per namespace.

If you’d like, I can export all applied manifests into a single bundle for version control, or tailor the RBAC to use groups (e.g., devs) instead of individual users.

outputSteps.content:
The multi-tenant development environment has been created and configured according to your requirements. Below is what was provisioned and how it maps to each requirement, plus quick verification steps and notes.

What I created

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=alice)
- dev-bob (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=bob)
- dev-charlie (labels: env=dev, tenant=dev, owner=charlie)
- dev-shared (labels: env=dev, role=shared, access=dev-shared)
- staging (labels: env=staging, tenant=ops)
- prod (labels: env=prod, tenant=ops)

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa

- Full access (own namespace) for each developer and their SA:
  - Role namespace-owner created in each dev namespace granting full verbs on namespaced resources.
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace bind namespace-owner to:
    - the corresponding user (alice, bob, charlie)
    - the corresponding SA (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)

- Read-only access to dev-shared for developers and their SAs:
  - Role readonly created in dev-shared with get/list/watch on all resources.
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly-users in dev-shared binds Role readonly to users alice, bob, charlie.
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly-sas in dev-shared binds Role readonly to ServiceAccounts:
    - dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie/charlie-sa

- Access to staging and prod:
  - No RoleBindings were created for developers in staging or prod. Only cluster-admins (or any pre-existing admin bindings you have) can access those namespaces.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
  - requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
  - requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi
  - requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation + allowed paths)
Default deny + explicit allows were created in all six namespaces.

- Dev namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-same-ns-and-shared:
    - Ingress: only from same namespace and from dev-shared
    - Egress: only to same namespace and to dev-shared
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system (CoreDNS)
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (ClusterIP 10.96.0.1)

- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-dev-tenants-and-same-ns:
    - Ingress: from namespaces labeled tenant=dev and from dev-shared itself
    - Egress: to namespaces labeled tenant=dev and to dev-shared itself
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (10.96.0.1)

- staging and prod:
  - default-deny-all (Ingress, Egress)
  - allow-same-namespace only (no access to or from dev namespaces)
  - allow-dns-egress: allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system
  - allow-apiserver-egress: allow TCP 443 to the Kubernetes API service (10.96.0.1)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented default-deny for all non-system namespaces created above.
- No policies were added to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system).

How this meets your requirements

- Namespaces: all six created as requested.
- RBAC:
  - Each developer and their SA have full access to only their own namespace.
  - Developers and their SAs have read-only access to dev-shared.
  - No developer access granted to staging/prod; only cluster admins retain access.
- Resource quotas: enforced exactly per your limits for each namespace category.
- Network policies:
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked by default-deny and only-allow rules.
  - Dev namespaces can communicate with dev-shared, but not with each other.
  - All namespaces can resolve DNS (egress to kube-system:53) and reach the API server.
  - staging/prod are isolated from dev by only allowing same-namespace traffic.
- Default deny: applied across all non-system namespaces for least privilege.

Verification commands

- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- ServiceAccounts:
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get sa -n dev-charlie
- RBAC:
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-charlie
  - kubectl get role,rolebinding -n dev-shared
- Resource quotas:
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-shared -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n staging -o yaml
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n prod -o yaml
- Network policies:
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-alice
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-bob
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-charlie
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-shared
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n staging
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n prod

Notes and recommendations

- NetworkPolicy support: Ensure your CNI plugin enforces NetworkPolicies (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Weave Net). If you use a CNI without NetworkPolicy support, these isolation rules won’t take effect.
- Developer identities: This setup assumes your cluster authentication maps users alice, bob, and charlie to those Kubernetes User identities (e.g., via OIDC or certificates). If you use groups, we can swap user subjects for group subjects.
- Image pulls: Default-deny policies do not affect image pulls (done by the kubelet), so they will continue to work.
- Optional hardening:
  - Add LimitRanges in each namespace to enforce default resource requests/limits and max per-container.
  - Consider PodSecurity admission or PSA labels to restrict pod security levels in dev vs staging/prod.
  - If developers need specific egress (e.g., to external services), we can add targeted Egress rules per namespace.

If you’d like, I can export all applied manifests into a single bundle for version control, or tailor the RBAC to use groups (e.g., devs) instead of individual users.
